one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes in response to a recent Pulse Asia survey (Sept 10-14, 2023) showing approval ratings for top officials -- President Marcos at 65 percent, VP Sara Duterte at 73, SP Migz Zubiri at 50, Speaker Romualdez at 41, and CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo at 34 -- and reflects on the broader pattern that no CJ has exceeded a 50-percent approval rating in the last fifteen or so years. He argues that unelected CJs should be excluded from such approval/awareness/trust/performance surveys when conducted under the same standards and metrics applied to elected leaders, because such surveys constitute 'embarrassment at least, or even harassment' for the CJs and the Supreme Court. He grounds the argument in constitutional asymmetry: while the President, VP, senators, representatives, and SC justices share three basic qualifications (natural-born citizenship, minimum age, ability to read and write), justices and judges are constitutionally required five additional qualities -- 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' plus 'Member of the Philippine Bar' -- that are not required of elected officials, who acquire office through popular mandate and political skills (with the Constitution not prohibiting the unschooled, dishonest, dropouts, sycophants, and criminals from running for top executive and legislative posts unless disqualified by a law or a final judicial decision). Of the five additional qualifications, independence is the most prized and is protected by security of tenure, removal only via impeachment ('and arguably, with my respectful dissent, through quo warranto'), and fixed compensation that cannot be reduced by Congress and continues into retirement until death. Jurists must judge cases according to what is just and humane after due process -- not like Pilate who condemned Jesus Christ according to the rule of the mob, or like the Spanish conquistadores who executed Jose Rizal according to the rule of the powerful. Independence may mean working against the popular: a senator or former president cannot be acquitted simply because of popularity or to avoid street rallies, and decisions cannot be influenced through kins, friends, admirers, critical media, investigative journalists, opinion writers, social media practitioners, or even approaches via spouses, children, close relatives, school chums, doctors, or fathers-confessors -- these must be avoided 'like a plague.' Because CJs were not elected by poll respondents and are 'politically unknown,' they will always rank low, so 'let us spare them the embarrassment, nay, the harassment of being badly perceived vis-à-vis our elected officials.' He closes with a warning he will self-quote in subsequent columns: 'I will fret the day if and when CJs would vie for popularity instead of independence, surrender to the mob instead of to the truth based on a fair trial, and judge wickedly to gain fame and favor instead of rendering justice though the heavens may fall.'
